title: Use real headings, not styled paragraphs
summary:
A

is styled with bold, italic or larger text to look like a heading. Use a real heading element so the structure is available to everyone.
problem:
A

element is styled with bold, italic or a larger font size so that it looks like a heading. Visually it works as one, but the code says it is ordinary text, so the heading structure is invisible to assistive technology.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users often move through a page by jumping from heading to heading. A styled paragraph is not in that list, so they miss the section and may not realize the page is divided up. Heading-based navigation in other tools can miss it too.
steps:
Find the

that works as a title for the content below it.
Replace it with a heading element at the right level, such as <h2> for a main section or <h3> for a subsection. Do not skip levels.
Move the visual styling into your CSS for that heading, and remove the inline bold, italic or font-size from the markup.

If the text is not really a heading, such as a pull quote or a note, leave it as a

and drop the heading-like styling.

whyItMatters: Headings are how people with screen readers skim a page, in the same way sighted visitors scan big text. The failure is of WCAG's info and relationships idea, that structure shown visually must also be in the code. That is a Level A criterion, the level accessibility regulations commonly build on. Real headings also help search engines.
howToCheck: Open your browser's accessibility inspector and look at the element. The role should be heading, not paragraph. A headings list in a screen reader or a headings extension should show it.
